name: Prostate problems: symptoms and seeing a GP
summary: Prostate symptoms are mostly urinary, such as a weak flow or going more often. Causes include enlargement, infection and cancer, and a GP can assess them.
keyPoints: The NHS describes urinary changes, such as a weak flow, trouble starting and needing to go more often, as the main signs of an enlarged prostate.
An enlarged prostate is not cancer and does not raise the risk of prostate cancer, but a man can have both at once.
Early prostate cancer often causes no symptoms, according to the NHS.
The NHS advises seeing a GP about difficulty peeing, blood in the pee, pain when peeing or not being able to pee.
NHS inform says being unable to pass any urine is a medical emergency and to phone 999 for an ambulance.

body.heading: What are the common prostate symptoms?
body.body:
The prostate is a small gland below the bladder in men. For an enlarged prostate, the NHS describes urinary problems as the main sign. These include trouble starting to pee, a weak flow, dribbling after finishing and needing to go more often, especially at night. Some men with an enlarged prostate have no symptoms at all. The NHS says the symptoms usually build slowly and may get worse as a man gets older.

Prostatitis, which is inflammation of the prostate, can cause pain or stinging when passing urine, straining to pass urine and needing to go more often. It can also cause pain in the penis, scrotum, testicles or bottom. Sudden bacterial cases can bring a high temperature, sweating, chills and pain between the testicles and the back passage.

The NHS says early prostate cancer often causes no symptoms. Later signs can include peeing problems, lower back pain, tiredness and weight loss.

body.heading: What can cause prostate symptoms?
body.body: The NHS says it is not clear what causes benign prostate enlargement, but it is thought to be linked to hormone changes as men get older. Prostate Cancer UK lists age, hormonal changes, a family history of enlarged prostates and other health conditions as possible factors. The NHS says prostatitis is usually caused by an infection, such as a urinary tract infection. It is not always known what causes long-term prostatitis. The NHS adds that needing to pee often at night or having a weak flow is common in older men and does not necessarily mean cancer.

body.heading: Does an enlarged prostate mean cancer?
body.body: An enlarged prostate is not prostate cancer, and Prostate Cancer UK says it does not raise the risk of prostate cancer. A man can have both at the same time. The NHS says most men with prostate symptoms do not have prostate cancer, though symptoms can sometimes be caused by more serious conditions, including cancer. Blood in the urine may be a symptom of an enlarged prostate, but the NHS says this is rare and it is usually caused by something else.

body.heading: When should a man see a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP for difficulty peeing, needing to pee more often, blood in the pee, pain when peeing or not being able to pee at all. It also advises seeing a GP if symptoms change, get worse or do not feel normal. A urologist writing for NHS England said men with intrusive urinary symptoms should see their GP for assessment and, if needed, referral. For blood in the pee, pain when peeing or being unable to pee, the NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111.

body.heading: What might a GP do?
body.body:
The NHS says a GP asks about symptoms and how they affect daily life. The GP may examine the tummy and genital area, and may feel the prostate through the wall of the back passage, which is called a rectal examination. A urine sample may be tested for infection. A blood test may check that the kidneys are working properly, and a PSA blood test may also be offered. The NHS says a PSA result cannot give a definite diagnosis of prostate cancer. Men are usually asked to keep a diary of what they drink and how often and how much they pee.

A specialist may see men whose prostate feels abnormal or whose PSA result is raised. Hospital tests can include a urine flow test, an ultrasound scan of the bladder and a camera test of the bladder called cystoscopy. If prostate cancer is suspected, the NHS says the next steps can include an MRI scan and sometimes a biopsy.

body.heading: What treatments are there for an enlarged prostate?
body.body:
The NHS says treatment depends on how much the symptoms affect daily life. Mild symptoms may need only monitoring, which is often called watchful waiting. Lifestyle changes can include drinking less alcohol, caffeine and fizzy drinks, drinking less in the evening, exercising and keeping to a healthy weight. Medicines include alpha-blockers such as tamsulosin, which relax the muscles of the bladder and prostate. Another group, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors such as finasteride, shrink the gland over time. Surgery is generally kept for symptoms that do not respond to medicines, and UK options include transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), HoLEP, water vapour therapy and GreenLight laser surgery.

For sudden bacterial prostatitis, the NHS says treatment is with antibiotics. For long-term prostatitis, a GP may refer a man to a urologist, and treatment can include medicines, physiotherapy or talking therapies.

body.heading: Which signs need urgent help?
body.body:
Being unable to pass any urine at all is called acute urinary retention. NHS inform treats it as a medical emergency, because urine backing up can damage the kidneys, and says to phone 999 for an ambulance. Other signs it lists include severe lower tummy pain and a swollen bladder that can be felt. A hospital leaflet says a man in this situation needs to attend an emergency department to have a catheter put in. The NHS enlarged prostate page gives the route as an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

The NHS says prostatitis can be serious and can need urgent medical help. A fever alongside urinary symptoms can point to a serious infection or sepsis.
